H1.text: A trampoline pushes harder the deeper you sink. A rubber band pulls harder the more you stretch it.

H2.text: These forces change at every point. But F times d needs one steady force.

H3.text: Diya squeezes a kitchen spring against a small block. The harder she squeezes, the harder it pushes back.

H4.text: She lets go. The push starts strong and fades to nothing. Which force do we use to find the speed?

H5.text: None of them alone. We add up every tiny push. Let's see how.

P1.text: For a steady force, the change in K was simply F times d.

P2.text: On a force against position graph, F times d is a rectangle. Its area is the work.

P3.text: A changing force makes a slope or a curve, not a rectangle.

P4.text: So cut the path into tiny steps. In each tiny step, the force is almost steady.

S1.text: Let's run it. A two kilogram block, against a spring squeezed by forty centimetres.

S2.text: The spring constant is fifty newtons per metre. So at the start, it pushes with twenty newtons.

S3.text: Release! The push fades to zero as the spring opens. The block shoots off.

S4.text: Slow-mo replay. Cut the push into four steps of ten centimetres.

S5.text: In each step, the force is almost steady. So the work is a thin strip: force times step.

S6.text: One point seven five, one point two five, point seven five, point two five joules. They shrink as the push fades.

S7.text: Add them up. Four joules. That is the area under the force graph.

S8.text: The block leaves at two metres per second. Half times two times two squared: four joules. The area equals the change in K.

D1.text: Now the proof, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. K is half m v squared. So the rate of change of K is m v times d v by d t.

D3.text: Step two. m times d v by d t is the force F. So d K by d t equals F v.

D4.text: Step three. v is d x by d t. Cancel the d t, and d K equals F d x.

D5.text: Step four. Add every tiny piece from start to end. The integral sign just means: add them all.

D6.text: So K final minus K initial equals the integral of F d x. The area under the F x graph.

T1.text: Remember this. For any force, the change in K equals the area under the force against position graph.

C1.text: Steady or changing? Side by side.

C2.text: A steady ten newton push over forty centimetres. A rectangle. Area, four joules.

C3.text: The spring push, twenty newtons down to zero, over the same forty centimetres. A triangle. Area, also four joules.

C4.text: Now you try. Which push gives the block more kinetic energy? Pause and decide.

C5.text: The same! Both areas are four joules. Only the area counts, not the shape.

R1.text: What if the force turns around? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. Force along the motion. The strip sits above the axis. Positive work.

R3.text: Two. Force against the motion. The strip sits below the axis. Negative work.

R4.text: Three. The net area is the area above, minus the area below.

R5.text: Four. That net area is the change in K. It can be positive, zero or negative.

K1.text: Your turn. On an F x graph, ten joules sit above the axis and fifteen below. Does the body end up faster or slower? Pause and think.

K2.text: Slower! The net area is minus five joules, so the body loses five joules of kinetic energy.

W2.text: A one kilogram body starts at rest. A force F equals four x newtons pushes it from zero to three metres. Find its speed.

W3.text: At three metres, the force is four times three, twelve newtons. The graph is a triangle.

W4.text: Area equals half times three times twelve. Eighteen joules of work.

W5.text: It started at rest, so its final K is eighteen joules.

W6.text: Half times one times v squared equals eighteen. v squared is thirty six. v is six metres per second.

X2.text: Many students multiply the final force by the distance. Twelve times three, thirty six joules.

X3.text: But the force was smaller for most of the path. Use the area: eighteen joules.

E1.text: Where is this asked? With a force given as a formula or a graph, asking for the work or the speed.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A two kilogram block moves along x under F equals eight minus four x newtons. At x equals zero, its speed is one metre per second. Find its speed at four metres. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. One metre per second.

A2.text: The force is positive up to two metres, then negative.

A3.text: Area from zero to two is plus eight joules. From two to four, it is minus eight.

A4.text: Net work is zero, so K is unchanged: one metre per second. Three is the top speed, at two metres.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. A spring's push fades as it opens. How do we find the work it does?

Y3.text: Two. What does area below the axis on an F x graph mean?

Y4.text: Three. A steady push and a spring push give the same area. Which gives more K?

N1.text: Next time: a stretched catapult and a raised tank hold energy without moving. Where is it hiding? Potential energy.
